planting.note: Separate rooted basal offsets in spring and tuck them into lean, fast-draining decomposed granite or rocky soil, keeping the narrow cylindrical leaves above the grit.

directions: Separate rooted basal offsets in spring and set them into lean, fast-draining decomposed granite or rocky soil on a slope where runoff never pools around the crown. This San Diego County and Baja California coastal native forms dense clumps of slender, pale green, finger-like cylindrical leaves and sends up tall wiry stalks of small white star-shaped flowers in late spring. Like other dudleyas it goes semi-dormant through the hottest, driest part of summer and should be kept nearly dry during that rest, resuming light watering only as fall temperatures cool. Grow it in a rock garden crevice, raised bed, or shallow container where the clustering rosettes can spread naturally by offsets.

planting.note: Divide offset rosettes or tuck seedlings into rocky, humus-poor soil on a slope or crevice in part shade to full sun; this species resents standing water around its roots.

directions: Divide offset rosettes or tuck young plants into rocky, mineral soil on a slope, cliff face, or crevice garden where water drains away instantly. Native to coastal and inland cliffs and chaparral slopes of southern California and Baja, this dudleya grows a single rosette or small cluster of fleshy, tapering, lance-shaped leaves that often blush orange-red when stressed by sun and drought. In late spring it sends up branched stalks topped with striking brick-red to orange tubular flowers, a color unusual among the mostly white- or yellow-flowered dudleyas. Give it some afternoon shade in hot inland gardens and withhold water through its dry summer dormancy to avoid rot.

planting.note: Separate clustered offsets in spring and plant in gritty, fast-draining soil in full coastal sun; this island species tolerates salt spray and shallow rocky pockets.

directions: Separate clustered offsets in spring and set them into gritty, fast-draining soil in a sunny, exposed site that mimics its native sea-bluff habitat. Endemic to California's Channel Islands and islands off Baja California, this dudleya forms freely branching clumps of pale green to grayish rosettes that spread into sizable colonies over time. Tall slender stalks bear small white to pale yellow star-shaped flowers in late spring, after which the flowering rosette dies back while surrounding offsets carry the clump forward. It handles salt-laden coastal air and thin rocky soil well, making it a good choice for seaside rock gardens and container plantings in mild climates.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container divisions in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species spreads by short stolons into tight rosette mats.

directions: Plant offsets or divisions in spring in lean, gritty soil with sharp drainage, in full sun to very light shade in hot climates. Native to rocky mountain slopes of Central Asia, this Rosularia forms flattened rosettes of pale green, finely hairy, spoon-shaped leaves that hug the ground and multiply steadily by short runners into a dense carpet. In summer, upright flowering stalks rise a few inches above the foliage, each bearing a loose cluster of small tubular white flowers. It is a favorite for alpine troughs, crevice gardens, and stone walls where excellent winter drainage keeps the fuzzy rosettes from rotting.

planting.note: Plant offset rosettes in spring in gritty, mineral soil in full sun; this Rosularia resembles a miniature Sempervivum and needs the same sharp winter drainage.

directions: Plant small offset rosettes in spring in gritty, mineral-rich soil with sharp drainage, in full sun. Native to rocky mountain habitats of Iran and Afghanistan, this species forms tight, fuzzy rosettes of fleshy leaves that shift from green to reddish-brown under bright light, closely mimicking a miniature hen-and-chicks. Clusters of small pink to whitish star-shaped flowers appear on short stems in summer, and the colony spreads gradually as new offset rosettes form around the base. It suits alpine troughs and crevice gardens where it can be kept dry and cool through winter.

planting.note: Plant offset rosettes in spring in lean, sharply drained gritty soil in full sun; each rosette is monocarpic and dies after flowering while offsets continue the colony.

directions: Plant offset rosettes in spring in lean, gritty soil with excellent drainage, in full sun. Native across Japan, Korea, China, and the Russian Far East, this Orostachys builds a tightly stacked, triangular-leaved rosette that gradually elongates into a distinctive cone shape as it matures, giving rise to its common dunce's-cap name. In late summer the mature rosette sends up a dense, pointed spike of small white to pink star-shaped flowers and then dies, while new offset rosettes clustered at its base keep the colony going year after year. It is a tough, cold-hardy choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, and shallow containers where winter wet is not an issue.

planting.note: Plant offset rosettes in spring in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Orostachys spreads readily by runners into a loose mat.

directions: Plant offset rosettes in spring in lean, gritty soil with sharp drainage, in full sun to very light shade. This Orostachys forms small, open rosettes of fleshy, gray-green to lavender-tinted leaves that spread readily by thin runners tipped with new plantlets, quickly covering bare rocky ground. In fall, mature rosettes push up a short, dense spike of small whitish flowers and then die back, leaving the surrounding offsets to carry the planting forward. It tolerates both heat and hard winter cold well, making it reliable in rock gardens, troughs, and gravel mulch beds.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun; this species, also sold as Lenophyllum pusillum, roots easily from broken stem segments.

directions: Plant stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light shade. Native to the Texas Gulf coast and northeastern Mexico, this low, clumping succulent produces small, plump, opposite leaves on sprawling stems that root wherever they touch soil, making it one of the easiest Crassulaceae to propagate and spread. Clusters of small yellow star-shaped flowers appear at the stem tips in warm weather, and the compact habit makes it well suited to rock garden edges, crevices, and shallow containers. It tolerates brief light frost once established but is best given winter protection or a sheltered microclimate in colder zones.
